Underrated new ideas
Before I edited Wired magazine, I edited the Whole Earth Review (formerly CoEvolution Quarterly). It was a magazine for conceptual news. We published new ideas. Since its demise, blogs and Substack in general have taken up that role. But starting a few years ago, a new magazine has appeared that is the closest replacement to Whole Earth. They publish new ideas. A couple of examples from recent issues: vaccinating wild animals, creating a rat-free city, using micro-bubbles to deliver drugs. Works in Progress is the only magazine I get delivered on paper; I enjoy reading its designed pages, and getting the extra bits you don’t get online. ⏪ He built a successful 45-person business. Then fired himself. Twice.
----------------------------------------------------------------------

Steve Kamb started NerdFitness.com in 2009 and grew it into a 7-figure business while leading a 45-person team.

Then he burned out. Hard.

He didn't want to lead a big team, so he demoted himself from CEO to Marketing Manager. But he was still miserable.

So he did something pretty drastic: He fired himself from his own business.

NerdFitness.com is still a successful business - but the big difference is Steve is not running it. He's not even involved in any of the day-to-day.

Instead, he's doing something that actually fills him up. He became an author and just released his second book.

And it's aptly titled How To Try Again ( https://2ed903a4.click.convertkit-mail4.com/d0u75493kkf0ho93gvpcmhz93l930szzvkm0n62xkggedzrkkmvr8d8328emeo307q6x586mrq85vpz5wxx8rqm502el0wq02opowx90dnvwx74vm7vr7d7zrqdb0zpp8/reh8h9uml7ek36t6u6/aHR0cHM6Ly9zdGV2ZWthbWIuY29tL2hvd3RvdHJ5YWdhaW4vP3V0bV9zb3VyY2U9Z3Jvd3RoaW5yZXZlcnNlLW5ld3NsZXR0ZXI= ).

How To Try Again
----------------

We had Steve on the podcast and he shared with us a helpful framework straight out of his book for how anyone can rebound from burnout.

Steve calls it the PACT framework. It stands for Pause-Accept-Change-Try.

How does it work, exactly?

Taking Steve's own experience as an example - first he had to Pause and realize what he was doing wasn't working. Steve calls this the "how to not make things worse" phase. Everything he'd been doing for years wasn't making anything better - he was more miserable than ever.

Steve couldn't work his way out of burnout. So he paused.

Then he had to Accept he wasn't cut out to be a CEO or a manager. He also had to accept he loved writing despite it not being a "normal" career path. In his book, Steve explains "why 'normal' isn't normal, and that's normal."

-----------------------------------------------------
I asked one of the big AI writing engines a question:
-----------------------------------------------------

“Can you describe meeting your firstborn child?”

----------------------------------------------------
The AI thought for a moment, then produced 88 words:
----------------------------------------------------

Meeting my firstborn child was a truly magical experience. It was a moment of joy and excitement that I will never forget. When I held my newborn for the first time, I felt a wave of love and warmth that I had not experienced before. I was filled with so much joy and pride that I was now a parent. My little one looked so peaceful and content in my arms. Seeing my baby for the very first time was an unforgettable moment that I will cherish forever.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I read it, then wrote my own description (limiting myself to the same 88-word count):
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

“He’s so quiet,” I said, looking up at the nurse.
​
She smiled behind her mask. We all wore masks. Gowns, too. Gloves and hairnets, too.
​
“Is that okay?” I said. “Is it okay he’s not crying?” I thought healthy newborns cried.
​
“It’s okay,” said the nurse. “He’s quiet but alert,” she said. “Just look at him looking at you.” I looked. “He’s looking right at you.” He was. He was looking in my eyes. “He’s saying hello,” she smiled.
​
“Hello,” I said. I felt like crying. “Hello, son.”

My son, Beau.

-----------------------------------------
AI can be a remarkable productivity tool.
-----------------------------------------

For example, I use AI as an instrument for sourcing and organizing ideas.

AI can help writers and copywriters establish the dots to help us start writing (which is often the hardest part).

But it cannot connect the dots like we can. It can’t be personal like us, human like us. It can’t feel the gravity of a profound moment, like a birth, much less the essence of another person. These are uniquely human experiences. And so, AI cannot write like us. It can’t tell stories like us. It can’t. Because the specifics, the details, the granularities we collect through our lived experiences belong to us.

The human condition—its nuances, its vastness—belongs to us.

----------------------------
So, will AI replace writers?
----------------------------

It will not.

AI may eventually replace some writing. But it cannot replace writers, people, everything we know and feel and emote.

We are, as it were, too much to bear.

Why Do Sales Hate Me?
*********************

This week, Talya joined us at Camp to lead a Bonfire on how to get sales to actually use what you build. Talya runs Down to a T, where she builds sales decks for B2B companies that help their champions sell them internally.

Here are the three biggest lessons I took away from her session.

------------------
The Discovery Trap
------------------

Many of our challenges start at the very beginning with how we complete our discovery sessions with sales. Maybe sales has been asking for extra support, or there's a new product launch that they need to be enabled for. So you hop on a call with the sales team and ask, "What do you need?"

This is the wrong question to ask because 99% of the time sales doesn't know what they need. They know what they want. And what they want isn't always what they need.

Wants are tactical. They sound like "I need a battlecard." Needs are goal-oriented. They sound like "I need buyers to stop stalling after the demo."

Talya recommends you ask these 4 questions instead:

​
This will help you properly complete narrative discovery before you jump into asset discovery. You're reverse-engineering how the buyers are going to make a decision, and then building your assets around that.

The format (deck, one-pager, interactive tool) matters less. What matters is the information...essentially, what the buyer needs to know to feel good about moving forward. If you address those early doubts and objections head-on in the assets, that almost guarantees sales will use them, because it helps them close.

----------------
The Handoff Test
----------------

Let's assume you've done your discovery well and built assets with a strong sales narrative. The reality is that you're probably not the one telling that narrative on the call. You build the story, but sales is the one who uses it. By the time it reaches the buyer, what they're hearing is the rep's translation of your work. Talya calls this the translation gap.

​
The story may be well-researched and comprehensive. But, then sales gets gets on a call and improvises. They lean on features and get deal-specific. So what the buyer hears is inconsistent with the story they saw on the website, and that often plants a seed of confusion.

While we may be tempted to blame sales, Talya says it usually isn't their fault. It's a story problem, meaning the narrative probably wasn't strong enough to survive the handoff. Sales will use what they believe in. And if they don't believe in your narrative, they won't use it. It's as simple as that.

​
We're obsessed with battlecards and competitors. But most of the time we're actually just losing to the status quo. Our story needs to be compelling enough to justify a change for the buyer.

----------------------
Measuring What Matters
----------------------

You've fixed the story and sales is using it! Hooray 🎉 But, now how do you know if it's working?

Many PMMs measure asset views and downloads, sales rep awareness scores, and usage in tools like Highspot or Seismic. Talya says none of those metrics will actually tell you whether the story is landing.

​
What she recommends you measure is:

* Whether the entire sales team is telling the same story
* Whether win rate and deal size go up when your story gets used
* Whether deals move faster when the story resonates
* And if the internal champion's pitch is connected to your story

If you want a quick gut check, Talya recommends a 3-Question Field Test. Ask a handful of reps these questions, separately:

* What's the #1 reason a buyer shouldn't choose us?
* What's the #1 reason they should?
* What does a champion say to their CFO when they're selling us internally?

If you get consistent and specific answers, that means your story made it through!

Talya left us with one question. If she sat in on your next three discovery calls, what story would she hear? And would it be the story you'd write if you were starting from scratch?

My actual take We built an entire decade of Marketing infrastructure on the assumption that influence always leaves a trace. Multi touch attribution, pixel tracking, last click models, all of it rests on the idea that if something convinced a buyer, somewhere there's a UTM to prove it. That was never actually true. It just happened to be mostly true for 20 years because the way people researched purchases, search engines and clickable links, was technically trackable. That was a coincidence, not a law of Marketing. AI chat just exposed how thin that assumption always was. So I don't think the answer here is "find a better tracking tool." I don't think one exists. The dark funnel isn't a gap you patch with cleverer tagging. It's a permanent feature of how buyers research things now, and treating it like a temporary inconvenience is going to waste a lot of people's time over the next 2 years. The real problem isn't measurement The part that actually worries me isn't the measurement problem. It's the positioning problem underneath it. The shortlist used to get built on your landing page and your retargeting sequence. Now it's getting built inside a chat window, based on whatever the model already believes about your category. You can't bid your way into that the way you bid on a keyword. You can't run a clever CTA test to fix it. The growth hacking playbook that won the last decade just doesn't transfer to a system that's synthesizing an answer instead of clicking a link. What does seem to move it is closer to old school PR than Performance Marketing. Consistency. Being described the same way across sources you don't own. Saying something specific enough that a model can quote it, instead of something safe enough that it gets skipped. That's a slower, less controllable game than the 1 most of us were trained on.
